> shipping - Docker, CI/CD, health checks, rollbacks, migrations
> beyond code - writing in your voice, market research, pitch decks

fork it, trim it, and have your own version running by tomorrow

begin with a single plan and a single rules pack
turning on all 286 skills at once is the quickest way to make it worse

whoever wires this in over a weekend spends the next quarter reviewing work instead of typing it

Everyone is chasing the next model.

The real edge is boring.

Build a harness around how YOU actually work.

Your agent already logs every session.

Every prompt.
Every tool call.
Every error.
Every token.

Almost nobody reads it.

This ONE prompt turns those logs into a dashboard and tells you exactly what to fix.

Paste it into Claude Code or Codex 👇

START OF PROMPT

Build me an observability dashboard (like Langfuse) from my own AI coding sessions over the last 7 days.

SOURCES (read only, never modify):
Claude Code: ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl
Codex: ~/.codex/sessions/**/*.jsonl and ~/.codex/history.jsonl

PRIVACY: Never print secrets, API keys or full prompts. Any snippet stays under 10 words with keys, paths, URLs and long IDs removed.

STEP 1: THE NUMBERS
Write a Python script using only the standard library. For each tool, calculate:
• Sessions per day, prompts, and tool calls by tool name
• Failed tool calls, grouped by tool and error type
• Models used and tokens per model per day (input, output, cache read, cache write)
• Tool call latency and session length at p50 and p95
• Biggest sessions by tokens, longest sessions, and retries (same call repeated after an error)
• Prompts sorted into task types: build, debug, deploy, research, writing, UI, review, other
• Sessions grouped by project folder, with subagent runs flagged
If something isn't in the logs, write "not logged". Never make up a number.
Save everything to harness-summary.json.

STEP 2: THE DASHBOARD
Build one self contained dashboard.html with a dark theme and animated charts:
• Top strip: tool calls, prompts, error rate, tokens, p95 latency
• Sessions table: tool, project, start time, duration, prompts, tool calls, errors, tokens, model. Searchable, sortable, filterable, with a toggle to hide subagent runs
• Click any session to see a timeline of every turn and tool call, marked ok or error, with duration
• Charts for sessions by project, tokens over time by model, and a model table with error rates
• Latency by tool and an error explorer grouped by tool and error type
• Health scores per session, clearly labeled "heuristic"
If the file gets too big, include only the top 200 sessions by tokens.

STEP 3: THE FIXES
Using only this data, write HARNESS.md with suggested changes to my CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md:
• Model routing: which model should handle which task type, based on what worked and what failed
• Tools: keep (used a lot, rarely fails), fix (fails often), cut (barely used)
• Skills: one skill for every task I repeated 3+ times, with a trigger line and steps
• Guardrails: my 3 most common failure patterns and a check that prevents each one
• Budget: my 5 biggest token drains and one change that cuts each
Back every suggestion with the sessions it came from.

STEP 4: REVIEW FIRST
Show me my 5 headline numbers and the proposed config changes as a diff. Change NOTHING until I approve.

END OF PROMPT

Run it once a week.

Change only what the data proves.

That's how your AI gets better every week while everyone else just waits for the next model.

We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

Most people think giving an LLM a prompt is enough to build an AI agent.

But a truly capable AI agent needs memory, tools, planning, decision-making, reflection and much more.

Here are 9 essential components of an AI Agent Architecture you should understand:

1. LLM — The Brain

The core reasoning engine that understands instructions, processes context and generates responses or decisions.

Examples: GPT, Claude, Llama.

2. Memory — Retains Context

Allows an agent to remember information and use it later.

- Short-term memory: Current conversation
- Long-term memory: User preferences and past interactions
- Episodic memory: Previous events and experiences

3. RAG — Knowledge Access

Retrieves relevant information from external knowledge sources and provides it to the LLM.

This helps agents work with private, domain-specific and updated information.

4. Tools — Action Executor

Gives agents the ability to interact with external systems.

Examples:

- Web search
- APIs
- Databases
- Calculators
- Email and messaging

5. Planning — Decides the Steps

Breaks complex goals into smaller, manageable tasks.

The agent understands the goal, creates a plan, executes steps and observes the results.

6. Reflection — Self-Improvement

Evaluates its own output, identifies mistakes and improves future attempts.

This helps make agent workflows more reliable.

7. Multi-Agent — Collaboration

Multiple specialized agents work together to complete complex tasks.

For example:

- Research Agent
- Coding Agent
- QA Agent
- Manager Agent

Each agent handles a specific responsibility.

8. Monitoring & Guardrails — Safety Layer

Keeps agent behavior controlled, reliable and aligned with defined rules.

Includes input validation, output filtering, safety checks, logging and auditing.

9. Human-in-the-Loop — Human Oversight

Humans review, approve, edit or reject important decisions before the agent proceeds.

Especially important for sensitive and high-impact tasks.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗜𝗚 𝗣𝗜𝗖𝗧𝗨𝗥𝗘:

An LLM generates intelligence.

Memory provides context.

RAG provides knowledge.

Tools enable action.

Planning creates direction.

Reflection improves results.

Multi-agent systems enable collaboration.

Guardrails provide safety.

Human oversight builds trust.

The real power of AI agents comes from how these components work together, not just from having a powerful LLM.

virals.name: Stanislav Sorokin
virals.text:
One prompt line moved Claude Code and Codex to a new algorithm 32 of 32 times. A red heart: 0 of 32.

A 31K-view post from @HowToPrompt__ says a DeepMind study found that a red heart image attached to a coding prompt makes AI pick a different solution method 100% of the time. So we tested it on Claude Code (Opus 5.5) and Codex (GPT-6.1 Terra): 64 runs, same Fibonacci prompt, with and without the heart.

→ Method changed by the heart: Claude Code 0 of 16, Codex 0 of 16
→ Method changed by "it must work for n up to 1,000,000": 32 of 32, a plain loop became fast doubling
→ Correct code: 64 of 64
→ Median time: Claude Code 10.8 s, Codex 19.4 s

The twist: the picture moved nothing and one number in the spec moved everything. When an agent picks the wrong approach, what is usually missing is a limit in the prompt, not a mood.

What limit do you write into the prompt before your agent starts?

Repost this now, because prompt superstitions spread faster than test runs.

Follow @stas_sorokin_ for numbers from AI systems running in real production.

We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

𝗔𝗡 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗜𝗦 𝗠𝗨𝗖𝗛 𝗠𝗢𝗥𝗘 𝗧𝗛𝗔𝗡 𝗝𝗨𝗦𝗧 𝗔𝗡 𝗟𝗟𝗠.

Most people think giving an LLM a prompt is enough to build an AI agent.

But a truly capable AI agent needs memory, tools, planning, decision-making, reflection and much more.

Here are 9 essential components of an AI Agent Architecture you should understand:

1. LLM — The Brain

The core reasoning engine that understands instructions, processes context and generates responses or decisions.

Examples: GPT, Claude, Llama.

2. Memory — Retains Context

Allows an agent to remember information and use it later.

- Short-term memory: Current conversation
- Long-term memory: User preferences and past interactions
- Episodic memory: Previous events and experiences

3. RAG — Knowledge Access

Retrieves relevant information from external knowledge sources and provides it to the LLM.

This helps agents work with private, domain-specific and updated information.

4. Tools — Action Executor

Gives agents the ability to interact with external systems.

Examples:

- Web search
- APIs
- Databases
- Calculators
- Email and messaging

5. Planning — Decides the Steps

Breaks complex goals into smaller, manageable tasks.

The agent understands the goal, creates a plan, executes steps and observes the results.

6. Reflection — Self-Improvement

Evaluates its own output, identifies mistakes and improves future attempts.

This helps make agent workflows more reliable.

7. Multi-Agent — Collaboration

Multiple specialized agents work together to complete complex tasks.

For example:

- Research Agent
- Coding Agent
- QA Agent
- Manager Agent

Each agent handles a specific responsibility.

8. Monitoring & Guardrails — Safety Layer

Keeps agent behavior controlled, reliable and aligned with defined rules.

Includes input validation, output filtering, safety checks, logging and auditing.

9. Human-in-the-Loop — Human Oversight

Humans review, approve, edit or reject important decisions before the agent proceeds.

Especially important for sensitive and high-impact tasks.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗜𝗚 𝗣𝗜𝗖𝗧𝗨𝗥𝗘:

An LLM generates intelligence.

Memory provides context.

RAG provides knowledge.

Tools enable action.

Planning creates direction.

Reflection improves results.

Multi-agent systems enable collaboration.

Guardrails provide safety.

Human oversight builds trust.

The real power of AI agents comes from how these components work together, not just from having a powerful LLM.

outsiders.name: Stanislav Sorokin
outsiders.text:
One prompt line moved Claude Code and Codex to a new algorithm 32 of 32 times. A red heart: 0 of 32.

A 31K-view post from @HowToPrompt__ says a DeepMind study found that a red heart image attached to a coding prompt makes AI pick a different solution method 100% of the time. So we tested it on Claude Code (Opus 5.5) and Codex (GPT-6.1 Terra): 64 runs, same Fibonacci prompt, with and without the heart.

→ Method changed by the heart: Claude Code 0 of 16, Codex 0 of 16
→ Method changed by "it must work for n up to 1,000,000": 32 of 32, a plain loop became fast doubling
→ Correct code: 64 of 64
→ Median time: Claude Code 10.8 s, Codex 19.4 s

The twist: the picture moved nothing and one number in the spec moved everything. When an agent picks the wrong approach, what is usually missing is a limit in the prompt, not a mood.

What limit do you write into the prompt before your agent starts?

Repost this now, because prompt superstitions spread faster than test runs.

Follow @stas_sorokin_ for numbers from AI systems running in real production.
